newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli Treasury sees slower growth until 2000.
newsitem.headline: Israeli Treasury sees slower growth until 2000.

text.p: The Israeli economy will grow somewhat faster in 1997 after a sharp slowdown this year, but it will not return to the fast-paced expansion seen in the first half of the 1990's, Treasury officials said on Sunday.

"In first half of the 1990s, gross domestic product (GDP) grew six to seven percent annually. This is not a normal phenomenon, it's not usual," said Tzippi Gal-Yam, head of economic research and state revenues at the Treasury.

In presenting the 1997 budget to parliament on Sunday, the Treasury forecast GDP growth of 4.0 percent next year. This is up from a projected 3.8 percent expansion for 1996 but is a big decline from 7.1 percent in 1995.

The Treasury expects business sector GDP to grow 4.5 percent next year. But private consumption, which fueled the economic boom in 1995 and the first half of 1996, will slow to just 1.8 percent next year, the Treasury estimated.
In 1996, private consumption is expected to increase 3.4 percent after growing 4.5 percent in 1995.

The outlook for the rest of the decade depends on whether the government can fully implement a series of economic reforms designed to boost Israel's flagging economy. These include a paring down of the public sector, a reduction in the tax burden and a narrowing of the budget deficit.
In the best-case scenario, the Treasury said, Israel could average a heady 5.1 percent annual growth pace from 1998 to 2000. Without the reforms, the rate would reach just 4.1 percent.

Treasury Director-General David Brodett attributed this year's slowdown to two factors. First, suicide bombings in February and March hurt tourism and sales by Israeli companies to the West Bank and Gaza Strip. Second, the strengthening of the shekel against the dollar made it difficult for Israeli companies to compete in foreign market. The Israeli currency, he said, would appreciate a real six to seven percent this year.
Nevertheless, he said the government could revive growth with relative ease. "The Israeli economy, despite all the discouraging developments of this year, is still a strong economy," he said.
The Treasury hopes fiscal measures will help reduce the country's swelling current account deficit in the balance of payments from an estimated 5.4 percent of GDP this year to 4.7 percent in 1997.

The Treasury is cautious about projecting inflation and provided no forecast for 1997 in its budget presentation on Sunday. Brodett would only say that consumer prices would rise less than 10 percent next year, versus 11.4 percent in the 12 months to September 1996.
